title: What Is Meenakari Work? History, Styles and Care
seoTitle: What Is Meenakari Work? History, Styles & Care
seoDescription: Meenakari work explained: the word's meaning, Persian and Mughal roots, Jaipur and Banaras styles, how to judge finishing, and care tips for home items.
excerpt: Where Meenakari comes from, how fired enamel differs from the Meenakari-style finish on chowkis, thalis and boxes, and how to check quality and care for it.
content:
In short

  • Meenakari is a Persian word for decorating a metal surface with coloured enamel, often explained as "placing paradise onto an object".
  • The craft came from Persia, the Mughals brought it to India, and Jaipur and Varanasi are its best-known centres.
  • Fired enamel Meenakari is costly jewellery work, while decorative Meenakari on thalis, chowkis and boxes is affordable and made for everyday use.
  • Look for clean edges, even colour and a flat base, and clean with a soft cloth without soaking wooden pieces.

Pick up a pooja thali, a dry fruit box or a festive chowki in almost any Indian market and there is a good chance the seller will call it "Meenakari". The word covers a lot of things.

Some are centuries-old enamel jewellery made in Jaipur workshops. Others are everyday steel plates and wooden bajots with colourful patterns that cost less than a box of sweets.

Both have their place. But if you buy, sell or gift these items, it helps to know what Meenakari work is, where it comes from and how to judge the piece in front of you. This guide covers all of that in plain language.

What does the word "Meenakari" mean?

Meenakari (also written minakari or mīnākārī) is a Persian word. According to the Wikipedia entry on Mīnākārī, it combines mīnā, linked to the word for heaven or paradise, and kārī, meaning to place something onto something else. Put together, it is often explained as "placing paradise onto an object". In practice, it means decorating a metal surface with coloured enamel.

In everyday Indian trade, the same word has stretched to cover any colourful, enamel-look decoration on metal, especially in floral and paisley patterns. That wider use is why you will see it on chowkis, thalis and dabbas as well as on jewellery.

Where did Meenakari come from?

Decorative enamelling is old. The detailed style we now call Meenakari is traced to Persia, with the art flourishing under the Safavids. The Mughals brought the technique to India and refined it, and over time Rajasthan and Gujarat became especially well known for Meenakari artefacts and jewellery.

Jaipur is the name most people link with the craft. A popular account credits Raja Man Singh of Amber with bringing skilled enamellers from Lahore to his court in the late sixteenth century. Treat the exact dates as tradition rather than settled history, but Jaipur's position as a major centre of enamel jewellery is not in doubt.

Regional styles worth knowing

  • Jaipur Meenakari: bold, saturated colours such as deep red, green and blue, usually on gold or silver jewellery and small objects.
  • Banaras Gulabi Meenakari: Varanasi's style is known for pink strokes on a white enamel base. Gulabi means pink. As NABARD's GI page on Gulabi Meenakari notes, the craft received a Geographical Indication (GI) tag in 2015, and the base metal, once gold, is now mostly silver and copper.
  • Decorative Meenakari on home and pooja items: the colourful patterned finish found on steel thalis, dabbas, bottles, and wooden chowkis or boxes with decorated metal sheet. This is the Meenakari most households use every day.

Fired enamel vs Meenakari-style decorative work

This is the point that confuses most buyers.

Traditional enamel Meenakari is made by fusing powdered coloured glass onto metal with intense heat. The Wikipedia entry puts the temperature at roughly 750 to 850°C. The powder melts into a smooth, glassy coating.

Each colour may need its own firing. That is why fine enamel jewellery is slow and expensive to make.

Meenakari-style decorative work on household items borrows the look: the same flowers, peacocks, borders and bright colours, applied to steel, brass or metal sheet that is fixed onto wood. These pieces are made for regular use and for gifting in quantity, so they are priced very differently from enamel jewellery.

Neither is "fake". They are different products for different jobs. A ₹100 steel pooja thali is not trying to be a Jaipur heirloom necklace.

If the method matters to you, for example because you are reselling and need to describe the item correctly, ask the manufacturer how the colour work on that particular product is done.

Fired enamel MeenakariDecorative Meenakari home items
Typical baseGold, silver, copperStainless steel, brass, metal sheet on wood
Common productsJewellery, small luxury objectsThalis, chowkis, dry fruit boxes, dabbas, bottles
Price rangeHighAffordable, suited to bulk gifting
Main useAdornment, collectingDaily pooja, festivals, return gifts, kitchen

Where you will see Meenakari work at home

Walk through a typical Gujarati or Rajasthani home during Diwali and you will spot the style in several places:

  • Pooja chowkis and bajots. Low wooden seats for idols, often covered with silver- or golden-finish Meenakari metal sheet. See the wooden chowki and bajot collection, or a piece like the Golden Meenakari Pooja Chowki.
  • Pooja thalis and plates. Steel thalis with a decorated rim or centre, used for aarti and festival rituals. Browse pooja articles such as the Meenakari Steel Pooja Thali.
  • Dry fruit and gift boxes. Wooden boxes with a Meenakari panel on the lid are a Diwali and wedding favourite. See the dry fruit box collection.
  • Jewellery and small gift boxes. Patari-style wooden boxes and small steel Meenakari dabbas in the jewellery and gift box range.
  • Kitchen items. Steel tiffins, bottles and dabbas with Meenakari designs in kitchen and utility.
  • Décor pieces. Occasional showpieces in home décor.

If you are trying to tell a chowki from a bajot or a patla, our guide to the difference between chowki, bajot, patla and chourang explains the names.

How to recognise good finishing

Whether you are buying one piece for your mandir or five hundred for a shop, the same checks apply. Look at the item in daylight and turn it over.

  1. Clean edges. On wooden items with metal sheet, the sheet should sit flat and the edges should be folded or finished so nothing sharp catches your finger.
  2. Even colour. Colours should stay inside the pattern lines without smudges, gaps or bubbles. Small variations are normal in handmade work; blotches are not.
  3. Secure fixing. Press gently on corners and borders. Nothing should lift, rattle or flex.
  4. Steady legs and flat base. A chowki should not rock on a flat floor. A thali should sit flat without wobbling.
  5. Smooth joints. On boxes, hinges and lids should open and close easily, and the lid should line up with the body.
  6. Consistency across a batch. For bulk orders, compare a few pieces side by side. Patterns and colours should match closely enough to sell or gift as a set.

How to care for Meenakari items

  • Wipe with a soft, dry or slightly damp cloth. Dry straight away.
  • For steel thalis and dabbas, wash gently with mild soap and a soft sponge. Avoid steel wool and harsh scrubbing on the decorated area.
  • Do not soak wooden chowkis or boxes in water. Moisture is the main enemy of wood.
  • Wipe off kumkum, haldi, ghee and oil soon after the pooja so they do not stain.
  • Store in a dry place, wrapped in cloth or paper, away from damp walls during the monsoon.

For thali-specific advice, read our Meenakari pooja thali guide.

Frequently asked questions

What is Meenakari work?

Meenakari means decorating a metal surface with coloured enamel. In everyday Indian trade, the word also covers colourful, enamel-look decoration on chowkis, thalis, boxes and dabbas.

What is the difference between Jaipur and Banaras Meenakari?

Jaipur Meenakari uses bold colours such as deep red, green and blue, usually on gold or silver. Banaras Gulabi Meenakari is known for pink strokes on a white enamel base and received a GI tag in 2015.

Is the Meenakari on a steel thali or wooden chowki real Meenakari?

It is decorative Meenakari, which borrows the look of fired enamel for everyday items. Neither is fake; they are different products for different jobs. If the method matters to you, ask the manufacturer how the colour work on that product is done.

How can I check the quality of a Meenakari item?

Check it in daylight for clean edges, even colour inside the pattern lines and secure fixing at the corners. A chowki should not rock, and a thali should sit flat.

How do I clean Meenakari items at home?

Wipe with a soft, dry or slightly damp cloth and dry straight away. Wash steel thalis gently with mild soap and a soft sponge, and never soak wooden chowkis or boxes.

title: Chowki vs Bajot vs Patla vs Chourang: What's the Difference?
seoTitle: Chowki vs Bajot vs Patla vs Chourang Explained
seoDescription: Chowki, bajot, patla or chourang? Learn what each low pooja seat is called across India, how they differ in shape and use, and which one suits your home.
excerpt: Four names, one family of low pooja seats. Here is what chowki, bajot, patla and chourang usually mean, where each name is used, and which one fits your need.
content:
In short

  • Chowki, bajot, patla and chourang are all low seats that keep an idol, kalash or person off the floor.
  • A chowki is usually a small square stand with four legs, and bajot is the common Gujarat and Rajasthan name for the same kind of piece.
  • A patla is lower, flatter and usually rectangular, while a chourang is the Maharashtra name for a square stool often used for Ganpati.
  • When you order, the size in inches and a photo matter more than the name.

Ask five families what they call the small wooden stand they keep under the idol, and you may get five different answers. In one house it is a chowki. Next door it is a bajot. A relative from Maharashtra calls it a chourang, and your grandmother insists the flat one is a patla.

They are all talking about close cousins of the same object: a low, raised seat that keeps something sacred or special off the floor. The names overlap a lot, and usage changes from region to region and even from family to family. Still, there are useful differences. Knowing them makes it easier to search, order or stock the right piece.

Why Indian homes use a raised seat at all

In Hindu worship, the deity is treated as an honoured guest. One of the traditional steps of puja, listed among the sixteen upacharas in the Wikipedia article on Puja, is asana, offering the deity a seat. A chowki or bajot is that seat in physical form.

It lifts the idol, kalash or photo above the floor and keeps it clean. It also marks out a small sacred space, even in a crowded room.

The same low seats are also used for people. During weddings, griha pravesh, Satyanarayan katha or other rituals, the person performing the pooja often sits on a patla. Many homes also use a small bajot as a stand for a diya, rangoli plate or decorative piece.

The four names, explained

Chowki

Chowki (also chauki) is the most widely understood word across North and West India. It usually means a small, square, four-legged stand with a flat top. When people search online for a "pooja chowki", this is what they want. Sizes range from tiny 2-inch pieces for a Laddu Gopal or a coin to 15-inch and larger stands for a main idol.

Examples: Pooja Chowki Meenakari (15x15 inch) and the Rajwadi wooden chowki.

Bajot

Bajot is the word you will hear most in Gujarat and Rajasthan. In practice a bajot is the same type of object as a chowki: a low, legged platform for pooja or décor. Many sellers, including us, list items as "bajot chowki" because buyers use both terms. Rajasthani and Rajwadi-style bajots often have more decorative legs, carved edges or a bolder metal finish.

Examples: Rajasthani Pooja Bajot, Mor (peacock) Bajot Chowki and the larger Khatli Bajot.

Patla and patli

A patla is generally flatter and more rectangular, sitting very low to the ground or on short legs. Traditionally it is a seat for a person during rituals or meals. It is just as often used to hold pooja items or to display something. A patli is a smaller patla.

Because it is long rather than square, a patla suits rows of items: a set of small idols, diyas for Diwali, or the bride and groom's seating in some wedding rituals.

Examples: Silver Meenakari Patla and the compact 6x4 Inch Patli Silver.

Chourang

Chourang (chaurang) is the term common in Maharashtra and among Marathi-speaking families. It is a square, four-legged stool, similar to a chowki, and is the usual seat for placing an idol at home during festivals such as Ganesh Chaturthi. Chourangs are often slightly taller and sturdier than small decorative chowkis.

Examples: Chourang Meenakari (8x8, 10x10 and 12x12 inch) and the 12x12 Chourang Wooden.

Side-by-side comparison

NameWhere it is commonly usedTypical shapeUsual purpose
ChowkiWidely understood across IndiaSquare, four short legsSeat for idol, kalash or photo
BajotGujarat, RajasthanSquare or rectangular, legged, often decorativePooja, festive décor, gifting
Patla / patliGujarat, Maharashtra and beyondLow, flat, usually rectangularSeat for a person in rituals; tray for several items
ChourangMaharashtraSquare, four legs, often a little tallerSeat for festival idols, especially Ganpati

Treat this as a guide rather than a rule. A Gujarati family may happily call a square stand a patla, and a Pune shop may sell the same piece as a chowki. When you order, the size in inches and a photo matter more than the name.

Materials and finishes you will come across

Whatever the name, these pieces come in a few common builds:

  • Plain wood. Simple, light and inexpensive, often used for small sizes or for people who want to cover the top with a cloth. See the pine wood chowki.
  • Wood with silver-finish metal sheet. The classic "silver chowki" look, with a bright patterned top that suits most mandirs.
  • Wood with golden-finish Meenakari sheet. Warmer, more festive, and popular for Diwali and weddings.
  • Metal frames or metal legs. For example the Metal Chourang Set and Chourang with metal legs.
  • Rexin-covered tops on some budget pieces, which are easy to wipe clean.

If you want to understand the Meenakari decoration itself, our article What is Meenakari work? explains how decorative Meenakari on home items differs from fired enamel.

Which one should you choose?

Start from the use, not the name:

  • One idol or kalash in a home mandir: a square chowki, bajot or chourang.
  • Several small idols, diyas or a row of items: a rectangular patla.
  • Somewhere for a person to sit during a ritual: a sturdy patla or a large, low bajot.
  • Festival idol such as Ganpati: a strong chourang sized to the idol's base.
  • Return gifts or shop stock: small decorative chowkis and patlis in matching sets.

Choosing the exact size, height and finish is a topic of its own. Our pooja chowki buying guide walks through measuring your mandir, matching size to the idol and the price bands to expect.

Ordering from Kalgi Handicraft

All of these, whatever you call them, are in our wooden chowki and bajot collection, made in Jasdan, Gujarat. Each product lists a starting price. You can order any quantity, from a single piece to a wholesale lot.

Not sure which name or size you need? Send an inquiry or WhatsApp +91 84698 85085 with a photo of your space or the item you have in mind, the quantity and your city. We will help you match it to the right piece.

Frequently asked questions

Is a bajot the same as a chowki?

In practice, yes. Bajot is the word used most in Gujarat and Rajasthan for the same low, legged platform, and bajots often have more decorative legs or a bolder metal finish.

What is a patla used for?

A patla is traditionally a seat for a person during rituals or meals. Because it is long and flat, it also suits a row of small idols or diyas.

What is a chourang?

Chourang is the Maharashtra name for a square, four-legged stool, similar to a chowki. It is often a little taller and sturdier, and is the usual seat for an idol during Ganesh Chaturthi.

Which stand is best for a Ganpati idol at home?

A strong chourang sized to the idol's base. We make chourangs in 8x8, 10x10 and 12x12 inch sizes, plus metal-legged options.

What should I use for several small idols or a row of diyas?

A rectangular patla works best, because it is long rather than square.

Can I order just one chowki?

Yes. There is no minimum order, so you can order a single piece or a wholesale lot. WhatsApp +91 84698 85085 with a photo of your space, the quantity and your city.

title: Pooja Chowki Buying Guide: Size, Height, Material and Price
seoTitle: Pooja Chowki Buying Guide: Size, Material & Price
seoDescription: How to choose a pooja chowki: measure your mandir, match size to the idol, pick height and finish, and see real price bands from ₹30 to ₹3,500 per piece.
excerpt: Measure first, then match the chowki to your mandir and idol. A practical guide to sizes, height, wood vs silver or Meenakari finish, care and real price bands.
content:
In short

  • Measure the shelf, the base of the idol and the clearance above before you choose.
  • Pick a chowki top at least an inch or two wider than the idol's base on every side, and leave room for a diya and flowers.
  • Go low for a cabinet or wall mandir; a taller, sturdy chowki suits a floor mandir or festival setup.
  • Starting prices in our range run from ₹30 for small 2x2 inch pieces to ₹3,500 for large statement pieces.

A pooja chowki looks like a simple purchase until you get it home and find it is too wide for the mandir shelf, too low to see the idol properly, or so light that it shifts every time you light a diya. A few minutes of planning avoids all of this.

This guide is about choosing the right chowki for a specific place and purpose. If you are still sorting out what chowki, bajot, patla and chourang mean, start with our explainer on the four names and come back here.

Step 1: Measure before you browse

Take a measuring tape and note three things:

  1. The space. Width and depth of the mandir shelf or the floor area where the chowki will stand.
  2. The base of what goes on it. The footprint of the idol, frame or kalash, not its height.
  3. The clearance above. In a wall-mounted or cabinet mandir, measure from the shelf to the ceiling of the mandir so the idol does not end up touching the top.

A simple rule: the chowki top should be at least an inch or two wider than the idol's base on every side, and the chowki should leave some room on the shelf for a diya and flowers. A stand that fills the shelf edge to edge looks cramped and is easy to knock over.

Step 2: Match the size to the use

Here is how common chowki sizes line up with typical uses, with real examples and starting prices from our catalogue. Prices are per piece and "starting from", so the final rate depends on the finish and quantity.

Top sizeGood forExamplesStarting price
2x2 to 5x5 inchLaddu Gopal, small murtis, coins, a single diya, return giftsWooden Pooja Chowki (2x2 to 5x5)from ₹30
6x6 to 8x8 inchSmall idols, kalash, photo frames in compact mandirs6x6 Chowki Metal Rexin, Golden Meenakari Pooja Chowki (8x8)from ₹80 to ₹145
10x10 to 12x12 inchMedium idols, Ganpati for home sthapana, a small group of idols12x12 Chourang Wooden, Chourang Meenakari (8 to 12 inch)from ₹120 to ₹130
15x15 inchMain idol in a floor or large wall mandir, festival setupsPooja Chowki Meenakari, 15x15 Inch Chowki BRfrom ₹400 to ₹420
18x18 inch and aboveLarge idols, havan or katha setups, statement piecesPooja Bajot & Meenakari Chowki, Khatli Bajotfrom ₹200 (wholesale) to ₹3,500

Price does not depend on size alone. A plain 15x15 can cost less than a heavily decorated 12x12. Finish, detailing and build all move the price.

Step 3: Think about height

Height is the measurement most people forget. A low chowki keeps a floor mandir calm and stable. A taller one lifts the idol to eye level when you sit for aarti, and makes a small idol stand out more.

  • Cabinet or wall mandir: go low, so the idol and any crown or flowers clear the top.
  • Floor mandir or festival setup: a taller chowki or chourang works well, as long as the legs are sturdy.
  • Stacking: some families use two or three chowkis of decreasing size to create steps. Check that the smaller one sits flat on the larger one.

Leg height is not always listed on product pages, so ask for it in your inquiry if it matters for your space.

Step 4: Choose the material and finish

Plain wood

Light, affordable and easy to cover with a red or yellow cloth. Good for daily use and for people who like to change the cloth for each festival. Our pine wood chowki is an example.

Silver-finish metal sheet on wood

The most popular look for home mandirs. A silver-coloured patterned top brightens the space and wipes clean easily.

One point to know across the market: "silver" in a product name usually describes the colour and finish, not solid silver. If you need real silver content, ask for it to be stated in writing on the quotation and invoice.

Golden or Meenakari finish

Warmer and more festive, with colourful floral or peacock patterns. Popular for Diwali, Navratri and weddings, and for gifting. Read more about the style in What is Meenakari work?

Brass and metal

Small brass chowkis like the 4x4 Inch Chowki have a traditional look and a bit more weight. Metal-legged chourangs such as the Metal Chourang Set are sturdy for heavier idols.

Step 5: Check the build

When the chowki arrives, or when you see a sample, check:

  • It sits flat with no rocking on a level floor.
  • The legs feel firm when you press down on each corner.
  • The metal sheet edges are smooth and lie flat.
  • The top is level, so a kalash with water will not lean.
  • For heavy idols, the top does not flex in the middle.

Caring for your chowki

  • Wipe with a dry, soft cloth after each pooja.
  • Clean kumkum, haldi, ghee and wax drips promptly. A slightly damp cloth works; dry it immediately.
  • Never soak or wash a wooden chowki under running water.
  • Keep a diya on a small plate rather than directly on the decorated top, to avoid heat marks and oil stains.
  • In the monsoon, keep it away from damp walls.

Buying for a shop or for gifting?

Retailers and return-gift buyers usually pick two or three sizes in matching finishes so they can offer a range. You can order any quantity, even one piece of each size, and the per-piece price usually drops for larger quantities. Our guide on buying handicrafts wholesale from a manufacturer explains how pricing works and how to write a quick, complete inquiry.

Find your chowki

Browse the full wooden chowki and bajot collection. If you are unsure about the size, send an inquiry or WhatsApp Kalgi Handicraft on +91 84698 85085 with your shelf measurements, the idol size, the quantity you need and your city. We will suggest options that fit.

Frequently asked questions

What size chowki is right for a home mandir?

Measure your shelf and the idol's base first. Choose a top at least an inch or two wider than the base on every side, while leaving space for a diya and flowers.

What size chowki do I need for Laddu Gopal?

A small 2x2 to 5x5 inch chowki suits Laddu Gopal and small murtis. Our Wooden Pooja Chowki in these sizes starts from ₹30 per piece.

How much does a pooja chowki cost?

Our starting prices run from ₹30 to ₹3,500 per piece. Finish, detailing and build move the price as much as size does.

Is a silver chowki made of real silver?

Usually not. "Silver" in a product name usually describes the colour and finish. If you need real silver content, ask for it to be stated in writing on the quotation and invoice.

How do I clean a wooden pooja chowki?

Wipe it with a dry, soft cloth after each pooja and clean kumkum, haldi or ghee with a slightly damp cloth, then dry it. Never soak it or wash it under running water.

Is there a minimum order for chowkis?

No. You can order any quantity, even one piece of each size, and the per-piece price usually drops for larger quantities.

title: Dry Fruit Boxes for Diwali, Wedding and Corporate Gifting
seoTitle: Dry Fruit Box for Gifting: Wholesale Buying Guide
seoDescription: Buying dry fruit boxes for Diwali, weddings or corporate gifts? Compare box types, match size to fill weight, plan your budget and know what to ask the maker.
excerpt: Compartment, jar or Meenakari? How to choose dry fruit boxes for bulk gifting, match box size to the quantity of dry fruits, plan your budget and time your order.
content:
In short

  • The main types are compartment boxes, jar-type boxes, Meenakari or decorative-finish boxes and themed designs.
  • Decide the fill weight and mix first, then confirm the usable capacity of each compartment with the maker.
  • Our dry fruit boxes start from ₹80 to ₹160 per piece, and the rate usually drops for larger quantities.
  • Plan backwards from the date you need the boxes in hand, and confirm production and dispatch time before you commit.

Sweets have always been part of Indian festive gifting. The Wikipedia article on Diwali notes the sharing of mithai and the sending of greetings with boxes of confectionery. Over the years, many families and businesses have added dry fruits to that list.

A good dry fruit box has become a gift in its own right. Unlike sweets, it stays useful long after the kaju and badam are finished.

If you are buying dry fruit boxes in bulk for Diwali, a wedding or a corporate order, the choice is more about planning than looks: the right type of box, the right size for the quantity you want to fill, and enough lead time. This guide walks through each step.

Who buys dry fruit boxes in bulk

  • Gift shops and dry fruit retailers who fill and sell boxes through the festive season.
  • Families planning weddings who need matching boxes for guests, relatives or return gifts.
  • Companies sending Diwali gifts to staff, dealers and clients.
  • Sweet shops and caterers who offer premium packing alongside their own products.

Each of them cares about slightly different things. A shop needs variety and margin. A wedding family needs a single design in a fixed number. A company needs consistency and a delivery date it can rely on.

Types of dry fruit boxes

Compartment boxes

Wooden boxes with a lid and two, three, four or more compartments inside. This is the classic format: a different dry fruit in each section, all visible when the lid opens. More compartments mean more variety but smaller portions of each. Our Dry Fruit Gift Box and 9x7 Dry Fruits Box are typical examples.

Jar-type boxes

A wooden stand or case that holds separate jars. Jars are practical for the person receiving the gift because they can refill and reuse them. See the 2 Jar Dry Fruit Box and the Dry Fruit Jar Box.

Meenakari and decorative-finish boxes

Boxes with golden-finish or Meenakari panels look festive straight away and need no extra wrapping. Options include the 2kg Golden Meenakari Dry Fruit Box and the Decorative Golden Finish Dry Fruit Box. If you want to know more about the style, see What is Meenakari work?

Themed designs

Some designs carry a motif, such as the Ram Mandir Dry Fruits Box or the 8x8 Amboj Elephant Dry Fruit Box. Themed boxes work well when the occasion has a clear religious or cultural focus.

Matching the box size to the quantity of dry fruits

This is where most bulk buyers go wrong. They choose the box first, then find it holds far less, or far more, than their budget allows.

Work the other way round:

  1. Decide the fill per box. For example 250 g, 500 g or 1 kg in total.
  2. Decide the mix. Two varieties suit a two-compartment or two-jar box. Four varieties need four sections.
  3. Ask for the capacity of each compartment. Box dimensions alone do not tell you this, because the depth of the compartments matters as much as the width. Light, bulky items like makhana need more space per gram than almonds or raisins.
  4. Test with a sample. Fill one box with your actual dry fruits and weigh it. This one step saves a lot of trouble on a large order.

A product name like "2kg" gives you an idea of the intended scale, but always confirm the usable capacity with the manufacturer for your specific mix.

Planning a bulk order: quantity and budget

Kalgi Handicraft has no minimum quantity: you can order a single box, which is useful for sampling, or thousands for a large gifting order. The per-piece price usually drops for larger quantities, so share your quantity when you ask for a quote. A few real examples from our dry fruit box collection:

title: Meenakari Pooja Thali Guide: What to Include and How to Care
seoTitle: Meenakari Pooja Thali: Contents, Types and Care
seoDescription: What goes on a pooja thali, how a steel Meenakari thali compares with brass or silver-plated, what a Karwa Chauth thali needs, and how to clean it safely.
excerpt: Diya, kumkum, akshat and more: what a pooja thali holds, why steel Meenakari thalis are popular, what a Karwa Chauth set includes and how to keep yours clean.
content:
In short

  • A pooja thali usually holds a diya, kumkum and haldi, akshat, agarbatti, flowers, prasad and water.
  • A steel Meenakari thali looks festive, does not rust and is easy to wash, so it works for daily use and gifting.
  • A Karwa Chauth thali set typically adds a karwa, a channi, a diya, sindoor, rice and sweets.
  • Clean it soon after use with a soft sponge and mild soap, skip steel wool on the decoration, and dry it straight away.

The pooja thali is the one item that turns up at almost every ritual in an Indian home, from the daily evening aarti to Diwali Lakshmi pooja, Raksha Bandhan and Karwa Chauth. It holds everything you need in one place and goes from hand to hand as the aarti is done.

Steel thalis decorated with Meenakari patterns have become a favourite because they combine a festive look with the practicality of stainless steel. Here is what goes on a pooja thali, how a Meenakari steel thali compares with other options, and how to keep it looking good.

What a pooja thali contains

There is no single fixed list, and every family has its own habits. The Wikipedia article on the puja thali describes the core items most traditions share:

  • Diya: an oil or ghee lamp for aarti.
  • Kumkum and haldi: usually in small bowls, for tilak and for marking auspicious symbols.
  • Akshat: unbroken rice grains.
  • Agarbatti or dhoop with a small holder.
  • Flowers: marigold, rose or whatever is offered in your tradition.
  • Prasad: sweets, fruit or a coconut.
  • Water in a small lota or kalash.

Many families add a bell (ghanti), camphor, sandalwood paste, betel leaves, tulsi or a coin. For festivals, the thali changes slightly: several diyas for Diwali, a rakhi and sweets for Raksha Bandhan.

If you are buying a ready thali set, check exactly which pieces are included. Some sets come with matching bowls and a diya; a plain thali is just the plate.

Steel Meenakari thali vs other materials

MaterialStrengthsThings to consider
Stainless steel with Meenakari decorationFestive look, does not rust, easy to wash, affordable for gifting in bulkTreat the decorated area gently when cleaning
Plain stainless steelVery durable, simplest to cleanLooks plain unless decorated with flowers
Brass or copperTraditional, weighty, much loved for daily poojaTarnishes and needs regular polishing
Silver-platedBright, special-occasion lookPlating can wear with harsh scrubbing
Decorated wooden plateLightweight, colourful, good for occasion-specific thalis like Karwa ChauthKeep away from water; wipe clean only

For everyday use and for gifting, a Meenakari steel thali is a sensible choice. It looks special enough for a festival and is tough enough for daily use. You can read more about the decoration style itself in What is Meenakari work?

Thalis in our range

  • Steel Meenakari Pooja Thali, from ₹100 per piece, a good pick for return gifts.
  • Meenakari Pooja Plate (medium), from ₹150 per piece.
  • Silver-plated Pooja Thali, from ₹100 per piece.
  • Stainless Steel Pooja Thali, from ₹150 per piece.

To complete the setup, look at the wooden agarbatti stand and small 4x4 pooja boxes for kumkum and haldi in the pooja articles collection. And if the thali will sit on a chowki in your mandir, our pooja chowki buying guide will help you pick the right size.

The Karwa Chauth thali

Karwa Chauth is observed by married women, mainly in North and West India, who fast from sunrise to moonrise for their husband's well-being. It falls on the fourth day of the waning moon in the month of Kartik, usually in October or November.

According to the Wikipedia article on Karva Chauth, the thali is central to the evening ritual. Women gather with their thalis, a lamp is lit, and sindoor, incense and rice are kept in it while the Karwa story is heard.

A typical Karwa Chauth thali set includes:

  • A decorated thali
  • A karwa (small spouted pot) for water
  • A channi (sieve) through which the moon, and then the husband, is seen
  • A diya
  • Sindoor, rice and sweets

The thali is used once a year and often photographed, so many women prefer a more decorative piece for this day.

Our Karwa Chauth Thali Set (Meenakari steel, from ₹350) suits shops and community buyers, while the Karwa Chauth Decorated Plate (from ₹350) works for individual orders. Ask which accessories are part of the set when you inquire.

How to clean and care for a Meenakari steel thali

  1. Clean soon after use. Ghee, oil, kumkum and haldi are easiest to remove while fresh.
  2. Use a soft sponge and mild dish soap. Wash the plain steel parts normally and go gently over the decorated area.
  3. Skip steel wool and scouring powder on the decoration. They can scratch the finish.
  4. Do not leave it soaking for long periods.
  5. Dry with a cloth straight away to avoid water marks.
  6. For haldi stains, a paste of baking soda and water on the plain steel area, rinsed after a few minutes, usually helps.
  7. Store flat, with a cloth or paper between stacked thalis so the decorated surfaces do not rub.

Wooden thalis and plates should only be wiped with a damp cloth and dried, never washed under the tap.

Thalis as gifts

A Meenakari thali is a thoughtful gift for griha pravesh, Diwali, a new bride or as a return gift after a pooja or wedding function. Pair it with a dry fruit box for a festive hamper; our dry fruit box gifting guide covers how to plan that in bulk.

Order pooja thalis from Kalgi Handicraft

Whether you need one thali or a few hundred for a shop or an event, send an inquiry or WhatsApp +91 84698 85085 with the design, the quantity and your city. Kalgi Handicraft is a manufacturer in Jasdan, Gujarat, and will confirm pricing and availability for your order.

Frequently asked questions

What items are kept in a pooja thali?

The core items are a diya, kumkum and haldi, akshat (unbroken rice), agarbatti or dhoop, flowers, prasad and water. Many families also add a bell, camphor, sandalwood paste, tulsi or a coin.

What is included in a Karwa Chauth thali set?

A typical set has a decorated thali, a karwa for water, a channi (sieve), a diya, and sindoor, rice and sweets. Ask which accessories are part of a set when you inquire.

Which is better, a steel or brass pooja thali?

Brass is traditional and weighty but tarnishes and needs regular polishing. Steel with Meenakari decoration does not rust, is easy to wash and is affordable for gifting in bulk.

How do I clean a Meenakari steel thali without damaging it?

Use a soft sponge and mild dish soap, go gently over the decorated area, and avoid steel wool or scouring powder. Do not leave it soaking, and dry it with a cloth straight away.

How do I remove haldi stains from a steel thali?

Put a paste of baking soda and water on the plain steel area and rinse it off after a few minutes.

How much does a Meenakari pooja thali cost?

Our Steel Meenakari Pooja Thali starts from ₹100 per piece and the Karwa Chauth Thali Set from ₹350. You can order any quantity, from one piece, and bulk orders usually get a lower per-piece price.

title: How to Buy Handicrafts Wholesale From a Manufacturer in India
seoTitle: Buy Handicrafts Wholesale From a Manufacturer
seoDescription: A guide for shops and gifting buyers: ordering any quantity, how 'starting from' prices work, what to put in an inquiry, samples, GST invoices and timelines.
excerpt: Order quantities, 'starting from' prices, samples, GST invoices and lead times explained, with a ready-to-send inquiry template for buying handicrafts direct from the maker.
content:
In short

  • Kalgi Handicraft has no minimum order: buy one piece or thousands, and the per-piece price usually drops for larger quantities.
  • A "starting from" price is the base rate; size, finish, quantity, design changes, packing, GST and transport set the final price.
  • Send one complete inquiry with the product, quantity, size and finish, delivery city and pin code, deadline, purpose and your GSTIN.
  • Confirm production time, transport, packing, payment terms and transit damage for your order before you commit.

If you run a gift shop, a pooja store or a return-gift business, buying directly from the manufacturer can give you better rates, more choice and a clearer answer when something needs to change. It also has its own vocabulary: order quantities, "starting from" prices, samples, GST invoices and lead times.

This guide explains each of these in plain terms and shows you how to write an inquiry that gets a useful reply the first time. We use examples from our own catalogue at Kalgi Handicraft, a manufacturer in Jasdan, Gujarat, so the numbers are real.

Why buy from a manufacturer at all?

  • Fewer layers. Each middleman adds a margin. Going to the maker removes some of them.
  • Direct answers. Questions about size, finish, packing or timing go to the people who make the product.
  • Range. You see the whole catalogue, not just what a trader decided to stock.
  • Repeat orders. Once you have a design that sells, you can reorder the same piece.

Many manufacturers only accept large production quantities. At Kalgi Handicraft that is not the case.

Order quantity: from one piece upward

Kalgi Handicraft has no minimum quantity. You can order a single piece or thousands. The per-piece price usually drops for larger quantities, so share your quantity when you ask for a quote.

Some real starting prices from our catalogue:

ProductStarting price

Agarbatti Stand₹20 per piece

A practical tip: if you are new to a product, order a few pieces first to test it with your customers, then move to larger wholesale quantities once you know it sells.

How "starting from" pricing works

When a product page says "from ₹100 per piece", that is the base rate for the standard version. The final price on your quotation can depend on:

  • The exact size and finish you choose
  • The quantity, since larger orders often get a better rate
  • Any change you request to the standard design
  • Packing requirements
  • GST, which is added on the invoice
  • Transport to your city

Treat the listed price as a guide for shortlisting, then ask for a written quotation for your exact quantity.

What to include in your inquiry

The fastest way to get a useful reply is to send everything the manufacturer needs in one message. Include:

  1. Product name or link, ideally the page URL or a photo.
  2. Quantity for each design. If you are flexible, give a range.
  3. Size and finish, for example 8x8 inch, silver or golden.
  4. Delivery city and pin code.
  5. Deadline: the date you need the goods in hand.
  6. Purpose: resale, wedding, corporate gifting, temple use. This helps the maker suggest suitable options.
  7. Your GSTIN, if you need a B2B invoice.
  8. Any special request, such as a custom size or branding, so the maker can tell you up front whether it is possible.

Here is a sample WhatsApp message that covers it:

Hello, I run a gift shop in Surat. I am interested in the 2 Jar Dry Fruit Box and the Golden Meenakari Pooja Chowki (8x8). I need about 200 of each, delivered to Surat 395007 by 20 September. Please share your best rate, dispatch time and whether you can give a GST invoice. My GSTIN is ...

Samples before a bulk order

For a large or first-time order, ask whether you can get a sample piece or recent photos and a short video of the same design. Check the finish, size and build against your expectations. If it is a box or thali for gifting, test it with whatever you plan to put inside. Ask whether the sample cost or courier charge is adjusted against the bulk order.

GST invoice questions to ask

If you are a GST-registered business, a proper tax invoice lets you claim input tax credit. Ask:

  • Will you issue a GST tax invoice with your GSTIN and the HSN code for each item?
  • What GST rate applies to this product?
  • Is the quoted price inclusive or exclusive of GST?

You can check any supplier's GST registration yourself on the official GST portal's Search Taxpayer page. Enter the GSTIN and confirm that the legal name matches and the status is active. Kalgi Handicraft is GST registered, and you are welcome to ask for our GSTIN when you inquire.

Timelines, packing and payment: ask, do not assume

These details vary by product, season and order size, so get them confirmed for your order:

  • Production time: when will the goods be ready to dispatch?
  • Transport: which transporter or courier, and who pays the freight?
  • Packing: how are pieces packed, and how many per carton?
  • Payment terms: advance, part-payment, balance before dispatch?
  • Damage in transit: what happens if some pieces arrive broken?

For festive orders, start the conversation well before your season. Our dry fruit box gifting guide covers planning around Diwali and weddings in more detail.

Checking a manufacturer before you order

  • How long have they been in business? Kalgi Handicraft was established in 1999 as a proprietorship firm and runs its own manufacturing and wholesale operation in Jasdan, with a team of 11 to 25 people.
  • Can you verify them independently? We have sold on IndiaMART for six years, where our rating is 4.5 out of 5 from 10 buyer ratings. Those buyers came from Ahmedabad, Surat, Vadodara, Rajkot and Jasdan in Gujarat, as well as Jabalpur, Hyderabad and Kathipudi.
  • Do they answer specific questions clearly? A good supplier tells you what is possible and what is not.
  • Is the address real? Ours is Aanand Nagar, Nr. New Bus Stop, Jasdan, Dist. Rajkot, Gujarat 360050.
